Porting a C++ hot loop from Rcpp to RZig

Source: vignettes/porting-rcpp.Rmd
porting-rcpp.Rmd

RZig is most useful when an R package has a small, computationally expensive loop that needs native performance but does not otherwise need C++. This vignette ports an axpy-style operation: return x + scale * y without modifying either R input. Every step up to the installation runs in R without a Zig compiler; the installation and the calls run when a supported compiler is found.

Start from the behavior, not the wrapper

An Rcpp implementation might duplicate x, validate the inputs, and mutate the duplicate in place:

#include <Rcpp.h>

// [[Rcpp::export]]
Rcpp::NumericVector axpy_rcpp(
    Rcpp::NumericVector x,
    const Rcpp::NumericVector& y,
    double scale
) {
    if (x.size() != y.size()) Rcpp::stop("x and y must have equal lengths");

    Rcpp::NumericVector result = Rcpp::clone(x);
    for (R_xlen_t i = 0; i < result.size(); ++i) {
        if (i % 100000 == 0) Rcpp::checkUserInterrupt();
        result[i] += scale * y[i];
    }
    return result;
}

The important contract is not the C++ class structure. It is that y is read only, x is duplicated before mutation, unequal lengths become an R error, and long computations remain interruptible.

Scaffold the Zig-backed package

Set the package path explicitly, then run use_rzig() once. This disposable example stays inside R’s session temporary directory; for a real project, replace package_path with its explicit package root:

package_path <- tempfile("yourpackage-", tmpdir = tempdir())
dir.create(package_path)
writeLines(
  c(
    "Package: yourpackage",
    "Type: Package",
    "Title: A Small RZig Example",
    "Version: 0.0.1",
    "Authors@R: person('Your', 'Name', email = 'you@example.org', role = c('aut', 'cre'))",
    "Description: Demonstrates a native implementation written in Zig.",
    "License: GPL-3",
    "Encoding: UTF-8"
  ),
  file.path(package_path, "DESCRIPTION")
)
scaffold <- use_rzig(package_path)
#> Generated RZig bindings for yourpackage: 1 exported function
#> Created RZig scaffold for package yourpackage
scaffold
#> RZig scaffold of package yourpackage: 52 files written
#> Zig source: src/rzig/src/main.zig
#> Exported functions: hello_zig
#> Next steps: edit main.zig, run document(), then install the package with a Zig compiler (see find_zig()).

use_rzig() creates the portable build files, the Zig source tree with the framework, a starter src/rzig/src/main.zig, and the generated R wrapper for the starter function. The Zig implementation of the port is shipped with RZig as inst/examples/axpy.zig; copying it over the starter file is the only edit the port needs:

main_path <- file.path(package_path, "src", "rzig", "src", "main.zig")
file.copy(system.file("examples", "axpy.zig", package = "rzig"), main_path,
  overwrite = TRUE)
[1] TRUE
cat(readLines(main_path), sep = "\n")
const std = @import("std");
const builtin = @import("builtin");
const rzig = @import("rzig");

pub const panic = if (builtin.is_test)
    std.debug.FullPanic(std.debug.defaultPanic)
else
    rzig.Panic;

/// Compute x + scale * y without changing either R input.
/// @param x The numeric vector to duplicate and update.
/// @param y A borrowed, read-only numeric vector.
/// @param scale The multiplier applied to y.
/// @return A new numeric vector containing the result.
/// @export
pub fn axpy(
    x: rzig.Mut([]f64),
    y: []const f64,
    scale: f64,
) rzig.Error!void {
    if (x.data.len != y.len) {
        return rzig.raise(
            "x and y must have equal lengths; got {d} and {d}",
            .{ x.data.len, y.len },
        );
    }

    for (x.data, y, 0..) |*result, value, index| {
        if (index % 100_000 == 0) try rzig.checkInterrupt();
        result.* += scale * value;
    }
}

comptime {
    rzig.registerModule(@This());
}

rzig.Mut([]f64) is the direct expression of copy-on-modify semantics. RZig duplicates and protects x before Zig receives writable storage. The y slice borrows R’s numeric storage as read-only memory. Because this function returns void, the generated boundary returns the mutated duplicate automatically.

The function contains no SEXP, PROTECT, C++ exception, or registration table. The types and @export marker supply enough information for RZig to generate those parts.

Inspect what R will see

scan_exports() reads the Zig source and lists every exported function with its R arguments and the R value of each parameter and of the result:

scan_exports(package_path)
#> Zig exports of package yourpackage (src/rzig/src/main.zig): 1 function
#> 
#> axpy(x, y, scale)
#>   x          rzig.Mut([]f64)        double vector, writable duplicate
#>   y          []const f64            double vector, borrowed
#>   scale      f64                    double, length 1
#>   returns    rzig.Error!void        the writable duplicate, a double vector

Generate the bindings

document() writes the Zig manifest, the R wrapper and the NAMESPACE block. Run it whenever an exported Zig signature or its documentation changes. The returned object holds the generated texts:

bindings <- document(package_path)
#> Generated RZig bindings for yourpackage: 1 exported function
cat(bindings$wrappers)
#> # Generated by rzig::document(). Do not edit.
#> 
#> #' Compute x + scale * y without changing either R input.
#> #' @param x The numeric vector to duplicate and update.
#> #' @param y A borrowed, read-only numeric vector.
#> #' @param scale The multiplier applied to y.
#> #' @return A new numeric vector containing the result.
#> #'
#> #' @export
#> axpy <- function(x, y, scale) {
#>   .Call(axpy_, x, y, scale)
#> }
cat(bindings$namespace)
#> # Generated by rzig::document(): begin
#> useDynLib("yourpackage",
#>   axpy_ = "axpy"
#> )
#> export("axpy")
#> # Generated by rzig::document(): end

rzig_status() checks every step and tells whether the generated bindings match the current Zig source and whether a supported Zig compiler is available for the installation:

rzig_status(package_path)
#> RZig status of package yourpackage
#>   [ok] DESCRIPTION   package yourpackage
#>                      SystemRequirements does not name Zig; state the
#>                        supported series, for example "Zig 0.16.x or 0.17.x"
#>   [ok] Scaffold      build files and framework sources present
#>   [ok] Zig source    src/rzig/src/main.zig
#>   [ok] Exports       1 function: axpy
#>   [ok] Bindings      generated files match the exports
#>   [ok] Zig compiler  /home/runner/work/_temp/0beafb3f-08c9-475d-9a85-dbeb3ad24ddb/zig-x86_64-linux-0.16.0/zig
#>                        (version 0.16.0)
#>   [ok] C toolchain   C compiler gcc

Check the signature before compiling

rzig_status() also rejects, before any compilation, the signatures the boundary cannot convert. A single-precision argument is one such case:

broken_path <- tempfile("brokenpackage-", tmpdir = tempdir())
dir.create(broken_path)
writeLines(c("Package: brokenpackage", "Version: 0.0.1"),
  file.path(broken_path, "DESCRIPTION"))
invisible(use_rzig(broken_path))
#> Generated RZig bindings for brokenpackage: 1 exported function
#> Created RZig scaffold for package brokenpackage
broken_main <- file.path(broken_path, "src", "rzig", "src", "main.zig")
cat("/// @export\npub fn half(x: f32) f32 {\n    return x / 2;\n}\n",
  file = broken_main, append = TRUE)
rzig_status(broken_path)
#> RZig status of package brokenpackage
#>   [ok] DESCRIPTION   package brokenpackage
#>                      R CMD check also requires Title, Description, License,
#>                        Authors@R
#>                      SystemRequirements does not name Zig; state the
#>                        supported series, for example "Zig 0.16.x or 0.17.x"
#>   [ok] Scaffold      build files and framework sources present
#>   [ok] Zig source    src/rzig/src/main.zig
#>   [--] Exports       `half`, argument `x`: type f32 is not supported; use f64
#>                      `half`: return type f32 is not supported
#>   [--] Bindings      out of date: manifest.zig, R/rzig-wrappers.R, NAMESPACE,
#>                        man/half.Rd; run document()
#>   [ok] Zig compiler  /home/runner/work/_temp/0beafb3f-08c9-475d-9a85-dbeb3ad24ddb/zig-x86_64-linux-0.16.0/zig
#>                        (version 0.16.0)

Build and call

build_zig() compiles and installs the package from a copy in the session temporary directory. It runs the checks of rzig_status() first, keeps the complete installation log, and on failure reports the first errors of the Zig compiler, the C compiler, the linker or the load test with their files and lines. The build needs a Zig compiler of a supported release series. The chunks below run when find_zig() finds one; this rendered copy of the vignette ran them.

build <- build_zig(package_path)
build
#> Build of package yourpackage: succeeded in 9.2 seconds
#> Zig compiler: /home/runner/work/_temp/0beafb3f-08c9-475d-9a85-dbeb3ad24ddb/zig-x86_64-linux-0.16.0/zig (version 0.16.0)
#> Installed into a library in the session temporary directory
package_name <- "yourpackage"
loadNamespace(package_name, lib.loc = build$library)
#> <environment: namespace:yourpackage>
axpy <- getExportedValue(package_name, "axpy")

The generated R function has the same three visible arguments:

x <- c(1, 2, 3)
y <- c(10, 20, 30)
result <- axpy(x, y, 0.5)
x
#> [1] 1 2 3
result
#> [1]  6 12 18
try(axpy(1:2, c(1, 2, 3), 1))
#> Error : rzig: argument `x` of axpy must be a numeric vector for rzig.Mut([]f64); got integer; use as.numeric() in R
sum(1:10)
#> [1] 55

The native error is an R condition, and the session remains usable. Integer vectors are rejected for numeric slices and mutable numeric inputs. Convert deliberately with as.numeric() in R rather than relying on an implicit native allocation.

What changes in the port

Rcpp’s NumericVector combines an R object, indexing, allocation, and mutation in one C++ class. RZig separates those capabilities. A borrowed []const f64 cannot mutate its input. rzig.Mut([]f64) duplicates before exposing writable storage. rzig.Ctx is used only when Zig-owned scratch or result memory is needed. Errors are explicit rzig.Error values, and the outer boundary turns them into R conditions after Zig cleanup has finished.

Generated packages compile in Zig’s ReleaseSafe mode. Bounds checks and integer-overflow checks therefore remain enabled in installed code. A failure is routed through RZig’s panic boundary instead of silently corrupting adjacent R memory.

Measure the boundary separately

Benchmark the algorithm and the language boundary as separate questions. For a hot loop, compare equivalent copy and mutation semantics, use the same compiler optimization level, warm each implementation, randomize execution order, and report distributions rather than one elapsed time.

The RZig repository includes tests/bench.R, which checks and times equivalent RZig, handwritten C, and Rcpp round-trip copies at lengths 1, 1,000, and 1,000,000. It records medians and interquartile ranges from randomized batches. This isolates conversion overhead from the workload being ported.

Port incrementally

Move one native function at a time and keep the surrounding R interface stable. Tests should cover empty and large inputs, missing values, wrong R types, length mismatches, and continued session use after each error. C libraries can coexist with Zig during a gradual conversion. C++ classes and templates usually need to be redesigned as Zig structs and explicit data flow rather than translated line by line.
